title: Ghost Hunters of the Ice: How a Glacier Became a Telescope
excerpt: I have to emphasize how lucky I was because when we started this project, everybody realized this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work—including myself. So this was kind of an adventure where success was not guaranteed, and we were lucky to overcome the various challenges. It was a long journey, but finally it worked.
content:
A Belgian, a glacier, and the shyest particle in the universe

Francis Halzen, a physicist from Belgium, laid the foundations for an entirely new kind of astronomy. Instead of collecting light with mirrors and lenses, he wanted to use the ancient glacial ice of the South Pole to catch some of nature’s most secretive particles: neutrinos. That idea became the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, an instrument that can follow neutrinos back toward the distant corners of the cosmos where they were born.

1

The particle that ignores everything

The neutrino is the shyest particle in the universe. It carries no electric charge and has almost no mass, so it barely notices ordinary matter. Walls, mountains and entire planets are practically empty space to a neutrino. It simply passes through.

Right now, every single second, about 65 billion neutrinos from the Sun are streaming through your little fingernail, and you feel absolutely nothing.

Not all neutrinos come from the Sun. Some arrive from much farther away, and those rare travellers carry clues to some of the biggest mysteries of the cosmos. If researchers can capture these cosmic neutrinos, they can work out what was happening in the extreme environments where they were created.

2

An idea born in the 1980s

Back in the 1980s, Halzen realised that the Antarctic ice sheet might be the perfect trap for enough of these elusive neutrinos to tell us where they came from. He quickly persuaded many others that the idea had real potential. In 1992, a determined group of researchers and engineers made their first attempts to lower light sensors down into the glacier at the South Pole.

The real breakthrough came roughly twenty years later. IceCube recorded neutrinos whose properties convinced researchers they had come from distant regions of space. The hunt for the universe’s neutrino sources had begun in earnest.

3

The hunt for high-energy neutrinos

Cosmic rays are tiny particles, mostly protons, that constantly race through space. Some carry astonishing amounts of energy, and scientists still do not know exactly where these powerful particles come from. It is one of astronomy’s oldest unsolved puzzles.

Neutrinos are a way to crack it. Broadly, scientists talk about two kinds. Low-energy neutrinos are produced by radioactive decay here on Earth, by the Sun and by nearby stars. Very-high-energy neutrinos, however, are thought to be born in powerful cosmic events far beyond our Solar System: exploding stars, the remnants of supernovae, and active galaxies. Studying these energetic neutrinos lets scientists peer into some of the most violent processes in the universe.

4

Radio sparks, flashes of light, and a meeting in Poland

In the 1980s, while Halzen was working on cosmic particles, he heard that Soviet researchers were planning to use radio receivers to catch neutrino signals in Antarctica. Their idea was that when a neutrino collides with an atom in the ice, it creates an electrical spark that gives off a radio wave. If that wave were strong enough, an antenna could pick it up.

Halzen was inspired, and he saw another possibility: install light sensors in the glacier ice and watch for the faint flashes of light produced by those collisions.

He contacted his research colleague John G. Learned, who was working on a similar project to catch light from interacting neutrinos in the deep, clear ocean water off Hawaii. Together the two physicists weighed the opportunities and the challenges of hunting neutrinos in Antarctica. They first presented their concept for a neutrino observatory in the South Pole ice in 1988, at a conference in Poland.

5

Why ice? The perfect, and terrible, location

Ice turns out to be a wonderful material for the job. Deep enough down, it is permanently dark. There is no interference from living creatures, only very low levels of radioactive substances, and the region is geologically stable with no earthquakes.

There is one big drawback. The cold makes it impossible to travel to or from the South Pole for most of the year. All the practical work has to be squeezed into the brief Antarctic summer, between November and February.

Even so, the idea was compelling enough that scientists from many different institutions joined Halzen to build a neutrino observatory in Antarctica.

6

Drilling with hot water

The first problem was how to put instruments deep inside the ice. Glaciologists had the answer: drill very deep holes by melting the ice with hot water.

A long cable carrying many light sensors could then be lowered into each water-filled hole before it froze solid again. Halzen likes to describe these sensors as light bulbs in reverse. Instead of turning electricity into light, they catch light and turn it into electrical signals.

7

The bubble problem

First, the team tested their idea by sinking sensors into the ice in Greenland, to check that they could register light from particles moving through ice. Then they started building the first neutrino observatory at the South Pole, called AMANDA.

But the upper layers of ice were full of tiny air bubbles. These scattered the light in every direction and blurred the information about how the particles were moving, so the very first attempts were disappointing.

Then came good news. Below about 1,400 metres, the ice turned out to be extraordinarily pure and transparent, because the enormous pressure squeezes the bubbles out of existence. Deep ice was actually excellent for detecting neutrinos.

AMANDA’s construction continued until January 2000. Everything worked as intended, but it was simply not big enough to catch the rare, energy-rich neutrinos from cosmic particle accelerators.

8

Going big: IceCube

A much larger volume was needed, so work began on a second observatory: IceCube. It instruments a full cubic kilometre of ice (1 km long × 1 km wide × 1 km deep) with 5,160 light sensors spread across 86 cables.

9

IceCube finally finds cosmic neutrinos

Researchers soon detected the first high-energy neutrinos, and a few years later they published the discovery of neutrinos that must have come from far outside our Solar System. The search for the universe’s neutrino sources could finally begin for real.

Every neutrino interaction that IceCube keeps collecting adds to our understanding of the violent settings where high-energy neutrinos are made, and could even reveal cosmic phenomena that nobody has imagined yet.

The ghost particle, explained simply

The word neutrino means “little neutral one” in Italian. Here is what makes it so strange, and so useful.

⊘

No charge

Electric and magnetic fields cannot push it around, so it travels in a perfectly straight line from its source.

◌

Almost no mass

Neutrinos are millions of times lighter than an electron. For decades physicists thought they might weigh nothing at all.

⇶

Barely interacts

A typical neutrino from the Sun could pass through a light-year of solid lead with a good chance of coming out untouched.

⟳

Shape-shifter

There are three types (electron, muon, tau), and a neutrino changes between them as it travels.

✺

Born in violence

The most energetic ones are created where cosmic rays smash into matter or light near black holes and exploding stars.

⌖

Points home

Because it is not deflected, the direction of a neutrino tells you where in the sky it came from.

Two kinds of neutrinos in this story

☀

Low-energy neutrinos

From radioactive decay on Earth, the Sun and nearby stars. Plentiful, but they tell us about our neighbourhood.

✸

Very-high-energy neutrinos

Believed to come from exploding stars, supernova remnants and active galaxies far beyond the Solar System. Rare, but they reveal the universe’s most violent engines.

Inside IceCube: catching a flash in the dark

IceCube never sees a neutrino directly. It sees the light left behind when, very rarely, one crashes into the ice.

①

Collision

A neutrino hits an atom in the ice and produces a charged particle, such as a muon or an electron.

②

Blue glow

That particle moves faster than light can travel through ice, creating a cone of faint blue “Cherenkov” light, like a sonic boom made of light.

③

Reverse light bulbs

Sensors on the cables catch the light. The timing of each flash reveals the particle’s direction and energy.

Why the Earth itself is part of the detector

IceCube is swamped by muons made when ordinary cosmic rays hit our atmosphere: roughly a million of them for every muon made by a neutrino. The clever trick is to look down. Almost nothing except a neutrino can pass through the entire planet, so particles travelling upward through the ice are very likely neutrinos that came in from the northern sky. The Earth becomes a giant filter.

From our source text

IceCube has already found a few potential sources of high-energy neutrinos. One of them is the active galaxy NGC 1068, also called M77. Of the neutrinos registered by IceCube, 79 appear to come from the direction of this galaxy, although more confirmation is still needed.

In recent years, IceCube researchers have also seen high-energy neutrinos coming from our own galaxy, the Milky Way. They expect these neutrinos arise when cosmic radiation collides with atoms in the thin gas between the stars.

The two Nobel Prizes behind the story

✪

Physics 2002

Raymond Davis Jr and Masatoshi Koshiba, for detecting cosmic neutrinos: Davis from the Sun, Koshiba from an exploding star in a neighbouring galaxy.

✪

Physics 2015

Takaaki Kajita and Arthur B. McDonald, for experiments in Japan and Canada showing that neutrinos change type, which solved Davis’s missing two-thirds.

One problem had lingered for decades: Davis caught only one-third of the neutrinos that calculations of the Sun’s nuclear reactions predicted. The answer turned out to be that there are three types of neutrinos, and they swap identities on their journey. In the end, the neutrino helped physicists confirm their models of what happens inside the Sun and inside a supernova.
